subject: maths
title: Chapter 2 · Test 4
summary: Fifteen questions on congruence proofs, similar triangles, circle properties, and networks: degree, trails and circuits, and shortest paths.
body:
This test covers Chapter 2: writing geometric proofs with congruent triangles, similar triangles, circle properties (angles and chords), and networks — vertices, edges and degree, paths, trails and circuits, and shortest paths.

Allow about 25 minutes. Work with no notes and no calculator unless a question says you may use one. Read every diagram carefully: diagrams are drawn to scale, but always use the numbers and markings given rather than measuring. Write your working on paper so you can check each step, then choose the best answer. Questions get harder as you go, and the last two are challenge questions.

questions.prompt: Which test shows that triangle KLM is congruent to triangle RST?
questions.explanation: All three pairs of sides are marked equal (one, two and three ticks), so the test is SSS. No angles are marked, so SAS and AAS can't be used.
steps: Match the tick marks: one tick, two ticks and three ticks in each triangle.
Three pairs of equal sides, and no angles are marked.

mistakes.B: Step 1: no angles are marked, so SAS can't be used.
mistakes.C: Step 1: neither triangle has a right angle marked.
mistakes.D: Step 1: AAS needs equal angles, but only sides are marked.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle KLM and a turned-over triangle RST. KL and RS have one tick, LM and ST two ticks, MK and TR three ticks. No angles are marked.

questions.prompt: Triangle DEF is similar to triangle ABC, with matching angles marked. Find x.
questions.explanation: k = 15 ÷ 6 = 2.5, so x = 4 × 2.5 = 10 cm. Adding 9 cm (giving 13 cm) treats the change as a difference.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the base grew from 6 to 15 by multiplying by 2.5, not by adding 9.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you multiplied 15 by 6 ÷ 4. Compare matching sides: 15 ÷ 6.
mistakes.D: Step 2: DEF is the larger triangle, so x must be longer than 4 cm. Multiply by 2.5.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle ABC with base AB 6 cm and side AC 4 cm, and a larger triangle DEF with base DE 15 cm and side DF marked x. Matching angles are marked with the same arcs.

questions.prompt: PQRS is a cyclic quadrilateral with ∠QPS = 67°. Find x, the size of ∠QRS.
questions.explanation: P and R are opposite, so x = 180° − 67° = 113°.
steps: All four vertices are on the circle, so PQRS is cyclic.
∠P and ∠R are opposite, so they add to 180°.

mistakes.A: Step 2: opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°; they are not equal.
mistakes.B: Step 2: doubling is for the angle at the centre. Here, subtract from 180°.
mistakes.C: Step 2: subtracting from 360° is for angles at a point. Opposite angles add to 180°.

questions.diagram_alt: A cyclic quadrilateral PQRS inside a circle. Angle QPS is 67° and the opposite angle QRS is x.

questions.prompt: How many vertices of this network have an odd degree?
questions.explanation: Degrees: A 2, B 4, C 3, D 2, E 4, F 3. Only C and F are odd, so the answer is 2. (The number of odd vertices is always even.)
steps: Find each degree: A 2, B 4, C 3, D 2, E 4, F 3.
The odd degrees are at C (3) and F (3).

mistakes.A: Step 2: 4 vertices (A, B, D, E) have EVEN degree. Count the odd ones.
mistakes.B: Step 1: recount B and E — each has degree 4. Odd vertices always come in pairs, so 3 is impossible.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 6 is the number of vertices. Only count those with odd degree.

questions.diagram_alt: A network with six vertices around a hexagon (A–B, B–C, C–D, D–E, E–F, F–A) plus edges B–F, B–E and C–E.

questions.prompt: A chord is 7 cm from the centre of a circle with radius 25 cm. Find x, the length of the chord.
questions.explanation: Half-chord² = 25² − 7² = 625 − 49 = 576, so the half-chord is 24 cm and the chord is 48 cm.
steps: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord; the radius 25 cm is the hypotenuse.

mistakes.B: Step 3: 24 cm is half the chord. Double it.
mistakes.C: Step 2: the radius is the hypotenuse, so subtract: 25² − 7². Adding gives about 26 cm, doubled to 52 cm.
mistakes.D: Step 2: you subtracted the lengths 25 − 7 = 18 and doubled. Square first.

questions.diagram_alt: A circle with centre O and radius OA of 25 cm. A dashed perpendicular from O to chord AB is 7 cm long. The chord AB is marked x.

questions.prompt: Which statement about routes through this network is true?

options.B: It has a Hamiltonian path but no Hamiltonian cycle

questions.explanation: P–Q–R–T–S visits all five vertices once, so there is a Hamiltonian path. P has only one edge, so no cycle can pass through it: no Hamiltonian cycle.
steps: P has degree 1: a cycle through P would need two edges at P, so there is no Hamiltonian cycle.
Try a path from P: P–Q–R–T–S visits every vertex once.
So there is a Hamiltonian path but no Hamiltonian cycle.

mistakes.A: Step 1: P has degree 1, so a cycle can't pass through P (it would need to arrive and leave by different edges).
mistakes.C: Step 3: P, Q, R and S all have odd degree — four odd vertices, so there is no Eulerian trail.
mistakes.D: Step 2: P–Q–R–T–S visits every vertex exactly once, so a Hamiltonian path exists.

questions.diagram_alt: A network with vertices P, Q, R, S and T. Edges: P–Q, Q–R, Q–S, R–S, R–T and S–T. P is joined only to Q.

questions.prompt: How much shorter is the shortest path from A to F than the route A–B–D–F?
questions.explanation: A–B–D–F = 6 + 4 + 7 = 17. The shortest path is A–C–B–D–E–F = 2 + 3 + 4 + 2 + 3 = 14. The difference is 17 − 14 = 3.
steps: Shortest path: A–C–B–D–E–F = 2 + 3 + 4 + 2 + 3 = 14 (A–C–E–F and A–B–D–E–F are 15).

mistakes.A: Step 2 only: 14 is the length of the shortest path. Subtract it from the length of A–B–D–F.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 15 (A–C–E–F or A–B–D–E–F) is not the shortest. A–C–B–D–E–F = 14 is shorter.
mistakes.C: Step 3: "how much shorter" means subtract, not add.

questions.diagram_alt: A weighted network with vertices A to F. AB 6, AC 2, BC 3, BD 4, CD 8, CE 10, DE 2, DF 7 and EF 3.

questions.prompt: In the diagram, AM = MB and CM = MD. ∠ACM = 44° and ∠AMC = 98°. Find x, the size of ∠MBD.
questions.explanation: △AMC ≅ △BMD (SAS: AM = BM, vertically opposite angles, CM = DM), with A↔B. So x = ∠MAC = 180° − 44° − 98° = 38°. 44° is the angle at D, not B.
steps: △AMC ≅ △BMD by SAS (AM = BM, ∠AMC = ∠BMD vertically opposite, CM = DM).

mistakes.A: Step 3: 44° is at C, which matches D. B matches A, so x equals the angle at A.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 98° is the angle at M. x is at B.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 180° − 98° = 82° is the two other angles together. Subtract 44° as well.

questions.diagram_alt: Segments AB and CD cross at M. AM and MB have one tick; CM and MD have two ticks. Segments AC and BD are drawn. Angle ACM is 44°, angle AMC is 98°, and angle MBD is marked x.

questions.prompt: Two similar triangles have perimeters of 18 cm and 27 cm. A side of the smaller triangle is 8 cm. How long is the matching side of the larger triangle?
questions.explanation: Perimeter is a length, so k = 27 ÷ 18 = 1.5 and the side is 8 × 1.5 = 12 cm. Adding 9 cm treats the change as a difference.
steps: Perimeters are lengths, so they scale by the same factor as sides.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the perimeter grew by 9 cm, but each side grows by the same FACTOR, not the same amount.
mistakes.C: Step 2: the larger triangle needs a longer side. Multiply by 27 ÷ 18, don't use 18 ÷ 27.
mistakes.D: Step 2: perimeters are lengths, so they scale by k = 1.5, not k² = 2.25.

questions.prompt: Triangle DEF is a reduction of triangle ABC. AB = 12 cm, DE = 4 cm and the area of ABC is 108 cm². Find the area of DEF.
questions.explanation: k = 4 ÷ 12 = ⅓, so the area factor is (⅓)² = 1/9 and the area is 108 ÷ 9 = 12 cm². Dividing by 3 only gives 36 cm².

mistakes.B: Step 2: you divided by k = 3. Areas scale by k², so divide by 9.
mistakes.C: Step 2: dividing by 27 uses k³, which is for volumes.
mistakes.D: Step 1: subtracting the 8 cm difference doesn't work for areas. Use the scale factor squared.

questions.diagram_alt: A large triangle ABC with AB 12 cm and area 108 cm², and a smaller similar triangle DEF with DE 4 cm and an unknown area.

questions.prompt: O is the centre of the circle and ∠OBC = 25°. Find x, the size of ∠BAC.
questions.explanation: OB = OC, so ∠OCB = 25° and ∠BOC = 180° − 50° = 130°. Then x = 130° ÷ 2 = 65°. Stopping at 130° gives the centre angle, not x.
steps: x = 130° ÷ 2 = 65° (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference).

mistakes.A: Step 2 only: 130° is ∠BOC at the centre. The angle at the circumference is half of it.
mistakes.C: Step 1: ∠OBC is a base angle of triangle OBC, not the angle at A.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 2 × 25° doubles the wrong angle. Find ∠BOC = 180° − 2 × 25° first.

questions.diagram_alt: A circle with centre O. A is at the top, B on the lower left and C on the lower right. Triangle ABC is drawn, and radii OB and OC. Angle OBC is 25° and angle BAC is marked x.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Euler and Hamilton routes in this hexagon network is true?

options.A: It has an Eulerian circuit but no Hamiltonian cycle
options.B: It has a Hamiltonian cycle but only an Eulerian trail, not a circuit
options.D: It has both an Eulerian circuit and a Hamiltonian cycle

questions.explanation: Every degree is even (A, C, E: 4; B, D, F: 2), so there is an Eulerian circuit, e.g. A–B–C–D–E–F–A–C–E–A. The outside A–B–C–D–E–F–A is a Hamiltonian cycle.
steps: Degrees: A 4, B 2, C 4, D 2, E 4, F 2 — all even, and the network is connected.
So there is an Eulerian circuit, e.g. A–B–C–D–E–F–A–C–E–A.
A–B–C–D–E–F–A visits every vertex once and returns: a Hamiltonian cycle too.

mistakes.A: Step 3: A–B–C–D–E–F–A visits every vertex once and returns, so there IS a Hamiltonian cycle.
mistakes.B: Step 1: B, D and F have degree 2 and A, C and E have degree 4 — all even, so there is an Eulerian circuit.
mistakes.C: Step 1 and Step 3: all degrees are even, and the outer hexagon is a Hamiltonian cycle.

questions.diagram_alt: A hexagon of six vertices A to F joined in order around the outside, with extra edges A–C, C–E and E–A forming a triangle inside.

questions.prompt: The weights are cycling times in minutes. Find the quickest time from S to T.
questions.explanation: S–B–D–C–T = 2 + 2.5 + 1.5 + 1 = 7 minutes beats S–A–C–T (7.5) and S–B–D–T (8).

mistakes.A: Step 2: 7.5 is S–A–C–T (or S–A–B–D–C–T). Starting S–B is quicker.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 8 is S–B–D–T. Going D–C–T (1.5 + 1) beats D–T (3.5).
mistakes.D: Step 2: 8.5 is S–A–B–D–T. Compare all routes and choose the smallest total.

questions.diagram_alt: A weighted network of cycling times in minutes from S to T. SA 1.5, SB 2, AB 1, AC 5, BD 2.5, CD 1.5, CT 1 and DT 3.5.

questions.prompt: In triangles ABC and DEF, AB = DE = 9 cm, BC = EF = 6 cm and ∠C = ∠F = 40°. Which conclusion is correct?

options.A: The triangles are not necessarily congruent, because the equal angle is not between the equal sides

questions.explanation: The equal sides are AB and BC, but the equal angle is at C — it is not between them. This is SSA, which can produce two different triangles, so congruence is not guaranteed.
steps: Equal parts: AB = DE, BC = EF, ∠C = ∠F.
The angle between AB and BC would be ∠B, but the given angle is ∠C — so this is "SSA".
SSA is not a congruence test: two different triangles can have these measurements.

mistakes.B: Step 2: in SAS the angle must be between the two sides. ∠C is between BC and AC, not between AB and BC.
mistakes.C: Step 1: only two pairs of sides are known to be equal, not three.
mistakes.D: Step 1: neither triangle is said to have a right angle.

questions.prompt: In a round-robin tournament, every team plays every other team exactly once. In a network of teams (vertices) and games (edges) there are 45 edges. How many teams are there?
questions.explanation: With n teams each plays n − 1 games, so the degree sum is n(n − 1) = 2 × 45 = 90. Since 10 × 9 = 90, n = 10.
steps: Each of n teams plays n − 1 games, so the sum of degrees is n(n − 1).
Sum of degrees = 2 × edges = 90, so n(n − 1) = 90.

mistakes.C: Step 1: 45 is the number of games (edges), not teams.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 90 is the sum of the degrees (2 × 45). Each team's degree is one less than the number of teams.
